entries.text: At 5:22 a.m., only the mixing desk, wall clock, and green-shaded duty lamp lit the control room. It was the station's last morning.
The bay was dark beyond the old windows, though the first ferry sounded offshore. Cape Hill Community Radio had awakened here for thirty-seven years before the final dawn.
I'm not late, am I? Three floors of stairwell lights went out, so I followed the handrail up; the schedule is still on last night's programs.
Somebody penciled ‘good morning’ underneath. I bet it was the woman from the convenience store; she always leaves us careful weekly weather notes about the coldest hour ahead.
We have eighteen minutes, enough to do this without rushing. Listen once before we decide; I cleaned up the last damaged section beside the silent tape deck.
I left every breath and pause where it was; sit here if you want. On your first morning shift, you claimed standing made you less nervous.
The transmitter lamp glowed without a flicker, tinting both their shadows red. During flooded roads and missing boats, the cape had watched that same light.
The summer wildfire was no different. There was no emergency today, yet the lamp would go dark one final time before sunrise was over the familiar rooftops.
So this really is our last shift. Packing the records last night felt like moving storage, but hearing the board alive makes this different.
Five years ago, when you moved me from student volunteer to the overnight desk, I thought this room would outlast both of us and all of its equipment.
Shutdown is at 5:40; the maintenance crew downstairs will disconnect the old transmitter then. Before that, the archive opens one sixty-second receiving window.
It is reserved for the station's final live broadcast. When it closes, finished or not, our frequency passes permanently to the coastal network after decades of local use.
You said we'd leave a station call in that window. I assumed you wrote it weeks ago, despite how often you revise even a power-cut notice.
Yet you postponed our final sentence until today. Do you have two versions and simply haven't told me which one you really want?
Not two versions—two answers. The archive accepts one uninterrupted transmission, and once it begins, it will not open a second take for us this final morning.
This is the archive's last record number for the old station. I meant to choose for everyone, but near shutdown it no longer feels like my decision alone.
Zhou took a reel from his canvas bag and placed it beside the deck. Damp had faded its paper label to a pale tea brown.
The thirteen-year-old date remained clearly legible, beside the hurried words ‘morning station call.’ A tiny surviving scrap of blue candy wrapper clung to one corner.
I found it at the back of storage, wedged between ferry cancellations and old request lists on the lowest shelf. That was my first morning shift alone.
I was too nervous to sleep, ate a mint before going on air, and stuck the wrapper there without thinking. Somehow it outlasted the schedule.
No wonder I didn't recognize you. Your voice was much brighter then, and every sentence tried to climb at the end through the small monitor speaker.
You spent years telling me to slow down and leave room around the words. I like knowing you also tried to fill every silence that morning.
Much faster, too. I thought one slow second would make someone miss the ferry, or keep a night worker from hearing that the road home had reopened.
The station manager held up a card behind the glass; it said, ‘Think of one person.’ So I read the whole call to a listener I had never met.
The reel began to turn, thirteen years of dim light passing around the clear housing. After a short hiss, a younger voice woke in the monitor.
A cart squeaked beyond the studio door; somewhere in the recording, a cup touched a desk. The whole vanished morning seemed to enter the room with it.
“This is Cape Hill Community Radio. Good morning. May someone hear you today.”
The words are old, but they don't sound far away. During a typhoon blackout, my mother waited beside a candle for this station to name a warm shelter.
Years later, as an intern, I learned that ‘may someone hear you’ was never just a slogan. You restored the tape without erasing the room around it.
I only joined the broken sections; I left the breaths, the turning paper, and the chair creaking. We carried things that looked too small for history.
A lost dog, ice on the hill road, an old man dedicating a song to his wife in hospital—what made them matter was another person beside the microphone.
After the final word, the level needle eased back to zero, though the reel turned another half-circle. Only the soft bed of tape noise remained.
It did not fall silent the instant the tide retreated; Lin did not ask Zhou to stop the deck. Zhou did not reach for it.
If the archive takes this recording, it remembers what the station used to be: your younger voice, the ferry still running, the neighbors phoning in road conditions.
It is complete, but I didn't even know you then. Do all the years we worked together remain on reels with no official record number?
Right—the other answer is to record something now, so the archive remembers us before shutdown. We would not summarize thirty-seven years or speak for everyone who left.
We would only say who is still in this room, and who they can hear. That would be honest, but the old call would return quietly to its box.
Can't we join them? Play the old call first, then let us answer it; sixty seconds is more than enough, and the past and present were never separate here.
Half the things you taught me came from somebody who once taught you. Why should the archive make us cut either side away now?
Because they preserve more than sound, including how it happened. One piece comes from thirteen years ago, and one comes from this final morning.
Splicing them makes a commemorative edit, not the station's last live transmission. We can pair them later, but this window will not let us avoid choosing.
Then we aren't choosing which one sounds better; we're choosing what we want the record to prove. The old voice shows that this room connected people again and again.
A new voice shows that, even at the end, someone remained to answer. Both are true; only the first sentence a future listener hears will change.
The clock reached 5:27, its second hand crossing a sun-bleached mark on the dial. Wind began tapping the rooftop antenna cable.
It sounded as if someone far away were knocking; downstairs, the maintenance crew moved a ladder across the floor below them. Thirteen minutes remained.
The old call carries what this place believed at the beginning: if you speak, someone may hear you. That was the station's earliest promise.
A new call carries our final lesson: listening is not one-way, and a reply keeps a station alive. One returns the promise; the other leaves an answer.
Both are true, and each is missing the other half, but our last shift cannot leave nothing behind simply because we cannot bear to lose either.
Don't make a future listener guess or decide only for who you were thirteen years ago. We are here today, and we can carry the choice together.
Lin pushed the send switch to standby. A relay answered beneath the console, and the deck and microphone lamps came on together under Lin's steady hand.
One lit the faded label; the other lit an empty sheet of paper. Beyond the window, dawn had reached the tip of the antenna.
The archive window permits one final transmission.
